name: aalib
why: Renders graphics as ASCII art via a portable library, a classic image-to-text transform with some charm.

brief.what_it_is: AA-lib is a portable ASCII art graphics library. It takes graphics drawing calls through a standard API and renders them as text characters, so programs can produce images on any terminal. The homepage describes it as a library that works on a terminal of any kind. The Homebrew package installs five executables built on it: aafire, aainfo, aalib-config, aasavefont and aatest.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's framing is simplicity: video cards, low-frequency monitors and crashing graphical apps cause many problems, and AA-lib is offered as the answer. The homepage says it gives old hardware more power.
brief.install_notes: The homepage gives no installation steps beyond the package. The download page (dated 2001) lists release candidate sources of version 1.4, plus a separate VGA library and text library that the DOS port requires, and an OS/2 patch. The Homebrew formula's executables are aafire, aainfo, aalib-config, aasavefont and aatest.
brief.standout: It is a 1990s-era text-mode rendering library whose origin story is a Linux penguin logo shown on Hercules monitors, converted to ASCII with a font-bitmap approximation table. The same author later made XaoS, a fractal zoomer, and the BB demo to show off the library.
brief.status: quiet. The newest news item is dated Apr 25 2001 (version 1.4rc4). The homepage says the project is moving from its original home to SourceForge and points to SourceForge news, which I did not fetch. I found no release or commit data for a recent version.
brief.caveats: The README is thin and the site is old. The online documentation and tuning pages were named but I found no URLs for them, so I did not follow them. Only release candidates from 2001 appear on the download page, and I could not confirm a current stable release. The site has a copyright notice from 1997 but I found no license text, so I cannot state the license. The Homebrew formula's caveats were empty.

entry.title: aalib
entry.tldr: A 1990s library that draws graphics as ASCII characters on any terminal, with a bundled demo that renders a roaring fire in text.
entry.deeper_look:
AA-lib is a portable graphics library whose output is text. Programs call a standard drawing API, and the library turns the pixels into characters on a terminal of any kind. The homepage puts it as: "It works on a terminal of any kind, it is fast and portable, it gives to you standard API."

The origin story is small and specific. The project began with a Linux penguin logo shown on Hercules monitors, converted to ASCII by matching regions of the image against a table that approximates font bitmaps. The author's stated motive is simplicity: video cards, low-frequency monitors and crashing graphical apps cause many problems, and the page says text output gives old hardware more power. Its closing line on the subject is "I vote for simplicity."

The idea underneath is that a character cell is a very coarse pixel, and picking the glyph whose shape best matches the patch of image behind it gives you grayscale from punctuation. Once you see that, every text-mode video player and terminal image viewer looks like a descendant. The same author later made XaoS, a fractal zoomer, and the BB demo to show off the library.

Homebrew installs five executables built on it: aafire, aainfo, aalib-config, aasavefont and aatest. The project is old, with its latest news item dated April 2001, but a library for drawing with text has little to go out of date.

try_this.what_happens: Runs the bundled demo, which draws a fire animation using only text characters.
Reports what AA-lib detects about your terminal and its display driver.
Shows the options for the test program that exercises the library's rendering.

entry.whats_unique: It is a text-mode rendering library from the 1990s with a standard drawing API, and it has a demo that is instantly recognizable. Many later ASCII renderers trace back to this idea.
entry.caveats: The project is quiet, with release candidates from 2001 on its download page, a thin README, and documentation pages I could not locate.
